newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ wages data no cause for concern - economists.
newsitem.headline: NZ wages data no cause for concern - economists.

text.p: New Zealand private sector wages data for the February quarter came in slightly above market expectations on Thursday, but economists said the inflation indicator was no cause for concern.
"I don't think it makes an awful lot of difference to the outlook, or to our anticipation of what the Reserve Bank will do," said BNZ economist Peter Jolly.

Statistics New Zealand said average ordinary time private sector earnings rose 1.1 percent in the February quarter and 3.6 percent in the February year. Financial markets had been expected rises in the order of 0.9 percent and 3.5 percent.
"It's obviously a bit higher than what the market had thought, but the important thing is it still represents a slight reduction in annual wage growth," Jolly said.
The 3.6 percent annual rise compares with a 3.8 percent increase in the year to November 1996.
The debt markets, bulled up prior to the 10.45 a.m. (2245 GMT) release, gave up their early gains but suffered no extensive damage.

"Nothing to get too excited over," a money market dealer said of the data. "There's been a small pullback, but you probably needed to see at least a 4.0 percent rise (in the year) for it to be of concern."
The 90-day bank bill rate rose to 6.93 percent from 6.89 percent before the wages data release, while the New Zealand dollar eased about 10 basis points to US$0.6874/81.
ANZ economist Bernard Hodgetts said while the deceleration in wage settlements was not as rapid as some people had hoped for, the wider picture of easing inflationary pressures remained intact.

"These things do tend to lag the wider economy anyway, and the signs from the labour market at the moment, with much slower employment growth and a slight pickup in unemployment, suggest that earnings will slow down," he said.
"I don't think, given the wider climate, that it's cause for too much concern."
He said the data did not change ANZ's prediction of a 50 basis point easing in the Reserve Bank's desired monetary policy line at the Monetary Policy Statement on June 27.
The private sector data were part of SNZ's Quarterly Employment Survey, the remainder of which has been delayed until June 12.
